name: Tours
summary: The Loire city of Saint Martin's shrine: see of Gregory of Tours, Alcuin's Carolingian abbey, goal of the Umayyad raid halted in 732, an Angevin and then royal town whose coin became France's money of account, and the residence of Louis XI.
overview: Tours, on the Loire in western France, grew around two centres: the Roman city with its cathedral, and the abbey town of Saint-Martin, whose shrine made it the leading pilgrimage city of Frankish Gaul. It was the see of Gregory of Tours, the abbey of Alcuin, a county town fought over by Blois and Anjou, and in the late fifteenth century the residence of Louis XI.
knownFor: The shrine of Saint Martin, the chief pilgrimage church of Frankish Gaul

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Tours lies on the south bank of the Loire, on the narrow strip of land between that river and the Cher, where the roads of western France crossed. The Roman town of Caesarodunum became the see of Martin, the soldier-saint whose tomb made Tours the greatest pilgrimage centre of Merovingian Gaul, and in the ninth century its abbey of Saint-Martin was one of the chief centres of learning in the Carolingian empire.

The medieval town had two hearts: the old walled city round the cathedral in the east, and the abbey town of Châteauneuf round Saint-Martin in the west, joined by a single wall only in the fourteenth century. Its counts were the rulers of Blois and then of Anjou, and from the middle of the fifteenth century Tours and the castles of Touraine were the favourite residence of the kings of France.

contentSections.title: Caesarodunum and Saint Martin
paragraphs: Caesarodunum, founded under Augustus, was a large open town with an amphitheatre. In the late third century it shrank behind a wall enclosing about twenty acres around the amphitheatre, the future cathedral city, and took the name of its people, the Turones. According to Gregory of Tours, its church was founded in the mid-third century by the missionary bishop Gatianus.

Martin, a former Roman cavalryman from Pannonia who was remembered for cutting his cloak in half for a beggar at Amiens, was chosen bishop of Tours by popular acclaim in 371. He founded the monastery of Marmoutier across the Loire, where he lived among some eighty monks. He died at Candes in 397, and his body was brought back by river and buried in a cemetery outside the town, where in about 470 Bishop Perpetuus replaced the small chapel over his grave with a large basilica.

contentSections.title: Gregory of Tours and the Merovingian city
paragraphs: The shrine became a pillar of the Frankish monarchy. After defeating the Visigoths in 507, Clovis came to Saint-Martin with gifts, and Gregory of Tours records that there he received letters from the eastern emperor naming him consul, put on a purple tunic and rode through the town scattering coins. Martin's cloak, the cappa, was kept by later Frankish kings as a relic, and the name of its keepers gave European languages the words chapel and chaplain.

Gregory himself, a Gallo-Roman aristocrat from the Auvergne, was bishop from 573 to 594. He rebuilt the cathedral after a fire and defended the sanctuary of Saint-Martin against Merovingian kings who wanted to drag out fugitives sheltering there. He also wrote the Ten Books of Histories, the main narrative source for sixth-century Gaul, and four books on the miracles of St Martin, which make Tours the best-documented town of Merovingian Francia.

contentSections.title: The battle of 732 and Alcuin's abbey
paragraphs: The wealth of Saint-Martin drew the Umayyad raid of 732. Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, governor of al-Andalus, led his army north past Poitiers towards Tours, and Charles Martel, mayor of the palace of the Franks, blocked the Roman road between the two towns in October. After days of skirmishing the Franks held against the Muslim cavalry, Abd al-Rahman was killed, and his army withdrew south by night. The Battle of Tours saved the shrine and strengthened the family of Charles Martel, whose descendants became the Carolingian kings.

Charlemagne gave the abbey to his adviser Alcuin of York in 796, and Alcuin spent his last years there until his death on 19 May 804. Under him and his successors the scriptorium of Saint-Martin produced corrected texts of the Latin Bible in large single volumes, written in a clear Caroline minuscule, and it became one of the most productive book workshops in the Frankish realm. The Vivian Bible, made in 845 for the lay abbot Count Vivian and presented to Charles the Bald on a visit to the abbey, is the most famous of them.

contentSections.title: Vikings, Châteauneuf and the counts
paragraphs: The Loire carried Viking fleets deep into the Frankish kingdom. Northmen sacked Tours, Saint-Martin and Marmoutier in 853, when the community carried Martin's relics to safety, and the abbey was attacked again in 903. In about 918 the canons of Saint-Martin surrounded their church and its houses with a wall, and this fortified abbey town, Châteauneuf, grew into a merchant quarter separate from the bishop's city to the east. Its lay abbots were the most powerful princes of the region, among them Hugh Capet, who became king of France in 987.

The county of Tours passed in the tenth century to the counts of Blois, and their long rivalry with the counts of Anjou ended in 1044, when Count Geoffrey II of Anjou defeated and captured Theobald III of Blois at Nouy and made him surrender Tours. Touraine then stayed Angevin for 160 years. In the same decades Berengar, master of the schools of Tours, taught that the bread and wine of the Eucharist did not change their substance, and councils at Rome, Tours and elsewhere condemned him between 1050 and 1079.

contentSections.title: Angevin and royal Tours
paragraphs: The counts of Anjou, and from 1154 the Plantagenet kings of England, held Tours from the castle beside the Loire bridge. In May 1163 the exiled pope held a great council in the city, attended by Thomas Becket and more than a hundred bishops. On 3 July 1189 Philip II of France and the rebel Richard the Lionheart took Tours from the dying Henry II of England, who submitted to their terms the next day and died at Chinon two days later.

Philip II completed the conquest of Touraine from Richard's brother John by 1205, and Tours became a royal town. Its coinage outlived the change of ruler: the silver penny minted by the abbey of Saint-Martin, the denier tournois, was adopted by the crown, and in 1266 Louis IX of France issued the gros tournois, making the livre tournois the most widely used money of account in France. The cathedral of Saint-Gatien, rebuilt in Gothic style from the 1240s, rose against the old Roman wall of the city.

contentSections.title: War, pilgrims and the court of Louis XI
paragraphs: The Hundred Years' War put Tours on the front line of the Loire. After the French defeat of 1356 the city and Châteauneuf were enclosed together by a single wall, completed around 1368. In April 1429 Joan of Arc stayed in Tours while Charles VII of France's armourers made her plate armour and a local painter made her banner, before she rode to relieve Orléans. On 28 May 1444 English and French envoys at Tours agreed the truce known as the Treaty of Tours, with the betrothal of Margaret of Anjou to Henry VI of England celebrated in the church of Saint-Martin.

Louis XI, who disliked Paris, made Tours his home. In 1463 he bought the manor of Montils just outside the town, rebuilt it as the castle of Plessis-lès-Tours, and ruled France from it until he died there on 30 August 1483. He gave Tours a mayor and aldermen in 1462 and brought silk weavers there in 1470, founding an industry that lasted for centuries. After his death the Estates General of 1484 met at Tours to settle the government of his young son Charles VIII.

contentSections.title: The medieval city
paragraphs: The city in the east kept the outline of the Roman fort: the cathedral, the archbishop's palace and the royal castle stood inside its walls, beside the stone bridge that crossed the Loire towards Marmoutier and the road to Paris. About a mile to the west, Châteauneuf grew around the basilica of Saint-Martin, rebuilt after fires in the eleventh and twelfth centuries as one of the largest churches in France, with double aisles and a ring of chapels round the choir. Between them lay fields, vineyards and the riverside abbey of Saint-Julien, which slowly filled with houses.

Tours' influence spread along the pilgrim and trade roads. It gave its name to the via Turonensis, one of the four roads to Santiago de Compostela described in the twelfth-century pilgrims' guide, and Martin's feast on 11 November, Martinmas, was kept across Europe as a day for paying rents and hiring labour. Thousands of churches from Scotland to Hungary were dedicated to him, and the livre tournois carried the town's name into account books all over France.
